**Setting up the condition.** Each group of three casts one vote, and there are $\binom{n}{3}$ groups, so the total number of votes is $\binom{n}{3}$. If every person receives the same number $v$ of votes, then

$$n\cdot v = \binom{n}{3} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}.$$

Such a $v$ exists exactly when $n \mid \binom{n}{3}$, which is equivalent to

$$v = \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{6} \in \mathbb{Z}.$$

**Divisibility.** The product $(n-1)(n-2)$ is always even, since it is a product of two consecutive integers. So the condition reduces to $3 \mid (n-1)(n-2)$, which holds exactly when $n \equiv 1$ or $2 \pmod 3$. Equivalently, $3 \nmid n$.

**Achievability.** Any person may be voted for regardless of group membership, so the $\binom{n}{3}$ groups only need to be split into $n$ classes of equal size $v$. This is possible whenever $n \mid \binom{n}{3}$.

**Counting.** For $10 \le n \le 100$ there are $91$ integers. The multiples of $3$ in this range are $12, 15, \dots, 99$, which is $\frac{99-12}{3}+1 = 30$ values. So the count is

$$91 - 30 = 61.$$

Check: $n=10$ gives $v=\frac{9\cdot 8}{6}=12$, which is an integer. $n=12$ gives $\frac{11\cdot 10}{6}$, which is not, and $12$ is excluded.

ANSWER: 61
